# Why metrics matter 📊 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## The danger of "good enough"
### When 99% accuracy is terrible

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Imagine a model that predicts whether a patient has a rare disease
- The disease affects [1 in 1,000 people]{.alert}
- A model that **always predicts "no disease"** achieves:
  - [99.9% accuracy!]{.alert} 🎉
  - But it catches [zero actual cases]{.alert} 😱
- This is the [accuracy paradox]{.alert}
- Accuracy alone can be deeply misleading
- We need [multiple metrics]{.alert} to understand performance
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![The accuracy paradox](figures/accuracy-paradox.png){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/accuracy-paradox.png"}

Source: [Medium](https://medium.com/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## What are we really measuring?
### Key questions before choosing metrics

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Every metric captures [one aspect]{.alert} of model performance
- There's no single "best" metric—it depends on [what you care about]{.alert}
- Key questions to ask:
  - What's the cost of a [false positive]{.alert}?
  - What's the cost of a [false negative]{.alert}?
  - Are the classes [balanced]{.alert} or imbalanced?
  - What [action]{.alert} will be taken based on the prediction?
- The choice of metric is a [design decision]{.alert} with real-world consequences
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Different metrics for different goals](figures/metrics-tradeoffs.png){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/metrics-tradeoffs.png"}

Source: [Analytics Vidhya](https://www.analyticsvidhya.com/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Class imbalance ⚖️ {background-color="#2d4563"}

## The reality of real-world data
### Most interesting problems are imbalanced

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Many real-world classification problems have [unequal class sizes]{.alert}
- Real examples:
  - **Fraud detection**: Only [0.2% of transactions]{.alert} are fraudulent
  - **COVID testing**: About [10% positive rate]{.alert} in tested population
  - **Manufacturing defects**: Different defect types have [very different frequencies]{.alert}
  - **Self-driving cars**: Pedestrians are [much rarer]{.alert} than other cars
- The minority class is often [the most important]{.alert} to detect!
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Class imbalance is everywhere](figures/class-imbalance.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/class-imbalance.png"}

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/2023/imbalance-outliers-shift/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Handling imbalanced data
### Techniques that actually work

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**Data-level approaches:**

- [Oversampling]{.alert}: Duplicate minority class examples
- [Undersampling]{.alert}: Remove majority class examples
- [SMOTE]{.alert}: Create synthetic minority examples by interpolating between existing ones
- [Balanced mini-batches]{.alert}: Ensure each training batch has equal class representation

**Algorithm-level approaches:**

- [Sample weights]{.alert}: Give minority examples more importance
- [Cost-sensitive learning]{.alert}: Penalise minority errors more heavily
- [Threshold adjustment]{.alert}: Change decision boundary after training
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Oversampling and undersampling](figures/oversampling-undersampling.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/oversampling-undersampling.png"}

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/2023/imbalance-outliers-shift/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Stratified sampling
### Preserving class balance in splits

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Random splits can create [imbalanced folds]{.alert}
- Example: 5% positive class might end up as 0% or 10% in some folds
- **Stratified sampling**: [Preserve class proportions]{.alert} in each fold
- Essential for [imbalanced classification]{.alert}
- Most ML libraries support this by default
- [Always use stratification]{.alert} for classification tasks!
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Stratified vs regular split](figures/stratified-sampling.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/stratified-sampling.png"}

Source: [Scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Classification metrics 🎯 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## The confusion matrix
### The foundation of classification evaluation

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- A table showing [all possible prediction outcomes]{.alert}
- Four key quantities:
  - **True Positives (TP)**: Correctly predicted positive
  - **True Negatives (TN)**: Correctly predicted negative
  - **False Positives (FP)**: Predicted positive, but actually negative (Type I error)
  - **False Negatives (FN)**: Predicted negative, but actually positive (Type II error)
- All classification metrics come from these four numbers!
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
| | Predicted + | Predicted − |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Actual +** | TP ✅ | FN ❌ |
| **Actual −** | FP ❌ | TN ✅ |

<br>

[![Confusion matrix visualisation](figures/confusion-matrix.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/confusion-matrix.png"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Accuracy
### Simple but dangerous

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Accuracy** = Proportion of correct predictions
- In words: [How often is the model right overall?]{.alert}
- Pros:
  - Intuitive and easy to explain
  - Good when classes are [balanced]{.alert}
- Cons:
  - [Misleading for imbalanced data]{.alert}
  - Doesn't distinguish between error types
  - Can hide serious model failures
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
**Example: Cancer screening**

- 1,000 patients: 10 have cancer, 990 don't
- Model predicts "no cancer" for everyone

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| TP | 0 |
| TN | 990 |
| FP | 0 |
| FN | 10 |
| **Accuracy** | **99%** |

[But we missed all 10 cancer cases!]{.alert}
:::
:::
:::

## Precision
### How trustworthy are positive predictions?

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Precision** = TP / (TP + FP)
- In words: [When the model says "yes", how often is it right?]{.alert}
- High precision = [few false alarms]{.alert}
- Important when [false positives are costly]{.alert}:
  - **Spam detection**: Don't want important emails in spam!
  - **Product recommendations**: Don't annoy users with bad suggestions
  - **Fraud prevention**: Don't block legitimate transactions
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Precision focuses on predicted positives](figures/precision.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/precision.png"}

Source: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precision_and_recall)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Recall (Sensitivity)
### How many positives did we catch?

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Recall** = TP / (TP + FN)
- Also called [sensitivity]{.alert} or [true positive rate]{.alert}
- In words: [Of all actual positives, how many did we find?]{.alert}
- High recall = [we don't miss many positives]{.alert}
- Important when [false negatives are costly]{.alert}:
  - **Disease screening**: Don't miss sick patients!
  - **Security threats**: Don't miss genuine attacks
  - **Safety systems**: Don't miss dangerous situations
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Recall focuses on actual positives](figures/recall.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/recall.png"}

Source: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precision_and_recall)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## The precision-recall trade-off
### You can't have it all

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Increasing precision usually [decreases recall]{.alert} and vice versa
- Think of it as a "strictness dial":
  - **Strict threshold**: Only predict positive when very confident
    - High precision, low recall
  - **Lenient threshold**: Predict positive more often
    - High recall, low precision
- The [optimal trade-off depends on your application]{.alert}
- Spam filter → favour [high precision]{.alert}
- Cancer screening → favour [high recall]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![The precision-recall trade-off](figures/precision-recall-tradeoff.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/precision-recall-tradeoff.png"}

Source: [Scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## F1 score
### Balancing precision and recall

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **F1 score** = Harmonic mean of precision and recall
- In words: [A single number that balances both metrics]{.alert}
- Why harmonic mean? It [penalises extreme values]{.alert}
  - If precision = 1.0 and recall = 0.01, F1 = 0.02
  - Arithmetic mean would give 0.505!
- F1 = 1 is perfect, F1 = 0 is worst
- Popular for [imbalanced classification]{.alert}
- Note: F1 is always [between precision and recall]{.alert}, but closer to the smaller value
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
**Example calculation:**

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Precision | 0.80 |
| Recall | 0.60 |
| **F1** | **0.69** |

<br>

**F-beta score**: If you care more about recall, use β > 1 (e.g., F2). If you care more about precision, use β < 1 (e.g., F0.5).
:::
:::
:::

## ROC curve and AUC
### Visualising classifier performance

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **ROC** = Receiver Operating Characteristic
- Plots [True Positive Rate]{.alert} vs [False Positive Rate]{.alert} at all thresholds
- Key features:
  - **Diagonal line**: Random guessing (worthless)
  - **Top-left corner**: Perfect classifier
  - **Area under curve (AUC)**: Overall performance
- **AUC interpretation**: Probability that a randomly chosen positive is ranked higher than a random negative

| AUC | Quality |
|-----|---------|
| 0.9–1.0 | Excellent |
| 0.8–0.9 | Good |
| 0.7–0.8 | Fair |
| 0.5–0.7 | Poor |
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![ROC curve example](figures/roc-curve.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/roc-curve.png"}

Source: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiver_operating_characteristic)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Quick exercise
### Which metric would you prioritise?

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}

**Discuss with your neighbour for 2 minutes:**

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=50%}
:::{.fragment}
**Scenario 1: Email spam filter**

- False positive = Important email goes to spam
- False negative = Spam in inbox

[Which metric: Precision or Recall?]{.alert}

:::{.fragment}
**Answer**: [Precision]{.alert}—missing some spam is better than losing important emails
:::
:::
:::

:::{.column width=50%}
:::{.fragment}
**Scenario 2: Airport security screening**

- False positive = Extra search (inconvenience)
- False negative = Threat goes undetected

[Which metric: Precision or Recall?]{.alert}

:::{.fragment}
**Answer**: [Recall]{.alert}—inconvenience is better than missing threats
:::
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Regression metrics 📈 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Measuring prediction error
### Intuitive comparison of metrics

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}

| Metric | What it measures | When to use |
|--------|------------------|-------------|
| **MAE** (Mean Absolute Error) | Average size of errors | All errors equally important; outliers expected |
| **MSE** (Mean Squared Error) | Average of squared errors | Large errors are especially problematic |
| **RMSE** (Root MSE) | MSE in original units | Same as MSE, but interpretable |
| **R²** | Proportion of variance explained | Comparing models on different scales |

<br>

:::{.fragment}
**Key intuition:**

- **MAE**: "On average, predictions are off by X units"
- **RMSE**: "Typical error size, but big errors count more"
- **R²**: "The model explains X% of the variation in the data"
:::
:::

## Choosing regression metrics
### Context matters

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**Example: House price prediction**

| Actual | Predicted | Error |
|--------|-----------|-------|
| £200k | £210k | £10k |
| £300k | £295k | £5k |
| £150k | £155k | £5k |

- **MAE** = £6.67k (average error)
- **RMSE** = £7.07k (larger errors penalised more)
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="margin-top: 20px;"}
> "The choice of metric should reflect the [real-world cost of errors]{.alert} in your specific application."

- Predicting delivery times? MAE is intuitive
- Predicting stock prices? Large errors are costly, use RMSE
- Comparing models? R² is scale-independent
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Validation strategies 🔍 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Why validation matters
### The problem of overfitting

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- A model that [memorises]{.alert} training data performs poorly on new data
- This is called [overfitting]{.alert}
- Signs of overfitting:
  - [Excellent training performance]{.alert}
  - [Poor test performance]{.alert}
  - Gap grows with model complexity
- We need to estimate [generalisation performance]{.alert}
- This requires [held-out data]{.alert} the model has never seen
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Overfitting visualised](figures/overfitting.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/overfitting.png"}

Source: [Scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Train, validation, and test splits
### The three-way split

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Training set** (~60-70%): Fit the model
- **Validation set** (~15-20%): Tune hyperparameters
- **Test set** (~15-20%): Final evaluation (touch once!)
- [Never look at test data during model development!]{.alert}
- If you tune on test data, you're [cheating]{.alert}
- The test set must remain [truly unseen]{.alert}
- For time series: Use [temporal splits]{.alert} (no random shuffle!)
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Train/validation/test split](figures/train-val-test.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/train-val-test.png"}

Source: [Machine Learning Mastery](https://machinelearningmastery.com/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Cross-validation
### Making the most of limited data

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- With small datasets, a single split may be [unreliable]{.alert}
- **K-fold cross-validation**:
  1. Split data into K equal parts (folds)
  2. Train on K-1 folds, validate on 1 fold
  3. Repeat K times, rotating the validation fold
  4. Average the results
- Common choices: K = 5 or K = 10
- Every data point is used for both training and validation
- More [robust estimate]{.alert} of generalisation
- **Leave-one-out CV (LOOCV)**: K = N (extreme case, computationally expensive)
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![5-fold cross-validation](figures/cross-validation.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/cross-validation.png"}

Source: [Scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Data leakage
### A silent killer of ML projects

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Data leakage**: Information from test set [contaminates]{.alert} training
- Common causes:
  - Pre-processing (scaling, imputation) before splitting
  - Feature engineering using future information
  - Duplicate data in train and test
  - Selecting features based on all data
- Result: Model looks great in development, [fails in production]{.alert}
- Prevention: [Always split first]{.alert}, then preprocess each split separately
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Data leakage destroys model validity](figures/data-leakage.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/data-leakage.png"}

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/2024/data-centric-evaluation/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Understanding overfitting ⚠️ {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Underfitting vs overfitting
### Finding the sweet spot

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Underfitting, good fit, and overfitting](figures/overfit-underfit.png){width="75%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/overfit-underfit.png"}
:::

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=33%}
**Underfitting** 📉

- Model too simple
- Poor on training AND test
- Can't capture the pattern
:::

:::{.column width=33%}
**Good fit** ✅

- Right complexity
- Good on both sets
- Captures true pattern
:::

:::{.column width=33%}
**Overfitting** 📈

- Model too complex
- Great on training, poor on test
- Memorises noise
:::
:::
:::

## Techniques to prevent overfitting
### Your toolkit

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}

| Technique | How it works |
|-----------|--------------|
| **More data** | Harder to memorise larger datasets |
| **Simpler model** | Reduce number of parameters |
| **Regularisation** | Penalise complex models (L1, L2) |
| **Early stopping** | Stop training before overfitting occurs |
| **Dropout** | Randomly disable neurons during training |
| **Cross-validation** | Detect overfitting early |
| **Ensembles** | Combine multiple models to reduce variance |

<br>

:::{.fragment}
> "All models are wrong, but some are useful." — [George Box]{.alert}
:::
:::

# Data-centric evaluation 🔬 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Underperforming subpopulations
### When overall accuracy hides problems

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Overall accuracy can hide [serious failures]{.alert} for specific groups
- **Real example** (2018 study):
  - Commercial face recognition error rates:
  - Light-skinned men: [0.8% error]{.alert}
  - Dark-skinned women: [34.7% error]{.alert}
- These are called [data slices]{.alert} or subgroups
- Always evaluate models [per subgroup]{.alert}, not just overall
- Even if you remove sensitive features, they may [correlate with other features]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Subgroup performance disparities](figures/slice-performance.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/slice-performance.png"}

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/2024/data-centric-evaluation/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Discovering where your model fails
### Error analysis

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**How to find underperforming subgroups:**

1. [Sort validation examples by loss]{.alert} (highest error first)
2. [Examine high-loss examples]{.alert}—what do they have in common?
3. [Cluster high-loss examples]{.alert} to find patterns
4. Inspect clusters for [common themes]{.alert}

**Example patterns you might find:**

- Blurry images
- Unusual lighting conditions
- Rare words or phrases
- Edge cases not in training data
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Error analysis workflow](figures/error-analysis.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/error-analysis.png"}

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/2024/data-centric-evaluation/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Why did my model get this wrong?
### Five common reasons

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}

| Reason | What to do |
|--------|------------|
| **1. The label is wrong** | Correct the annotation (model may be right!) |
| **2. Doesn't belong to any class** | Add an "Other" class or remove from dataset |
| **3. It's an outlier** | Collect more similar examples, or remove if rare |
| **4. Wrong model type** | Try different architectures or hyperparameters |
| **5. Conflicting labels in data** | Improve labelling guidelines, add distinguishing features |

<br>

:::{.fragment}
> Before blaming your model, [check your data]{.alert}! Many "model failures" are actually data problems.
:::
:::

## Outliers in ML
### Unusual data points

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Outliers**: Data points that differ significantly from others
- Common causes:
  - Measurement errors (faulty sensor)
  - Bad data collection (missing fields)
  - Malicious inputs (adversarial examples)
  - Rare but valid events (albino animal)
- [Don't blindly delete outliers!]{.alert}
  - They might be rare but valid
  - Have a domain expert review them
- Outliers can harm training or cause bad predictions at deployment
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![An outlier example](figures/outlier-example.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/outlier-example.png"}

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/2023/imbalance-outliers-shift/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Distribution shift
### When train ≠ test

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**Three types of distribution shift:**

1. **Covariate shift** (inputs change)
   - Self-driving car: Trained on sunny SF, deployed in snowy Boston
   - Input distribution changes, but relationship with labels doesn't

2. **Concept shift** (relationships change)
   - Stock prediction: What drove prices in 1975 ≠ 2025
   - Same inputs, different outputs over time

3. **Label shift** (class frequencies change)
   - Spam filter: Trained on 50/50, deployed where 90% is spam
   - Class proportions change
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Distribution shift example](figures/distribution-shift.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/distribution-shift.png"}

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/2023/imbalance-outliers-shift/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Addressing distribution shift
### Practical solutions

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}

| Strategy | How it works |
|----------|--------------|
| **Monitor performance** | Track metrics over time; detect degradation |
| **Monitor data** | Compare statistics of deployment vs training data |
| **Re-train regularly** | Update model with fresh data |
| **Weight training data** | Make training distribution match deployment |
| **Collect better data** | Sample training data that matches deployment conditions |

<br>

:::{.fragment}
> Distribution shift is present in [nearly every real-world ML application]{.alert}. Plan for it from the start!
:::
:::

# Ethical considerations 🤔 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## When metrics go wrong
### The dangers of metric fixation

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Goodhart's Law]{.alert}: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"
- Optimising for one metric can [harm other outcomes]{.alert}
- Examples:
  - Optimising for engagement → addictive content
  - Optimising for clicks → clickbait
  - Optimising for efficiency → job losses
- Metrics can be [gamed]{.alert} or [manipulated]{.alert}
- Real-world impact often [isn't captured]{.alert} by standard metrics
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Goodhart's Law in action](figures/goodharts-law.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/goodharts-law.png"}

Source: [Thomas & Uminsky (2022)](https://www.cell.com/patterns/fulltext/S2666-3899(22)00056-3)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Fairness metrics
### Equity in model performance

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Overall accuracy can hide [disparate performance]{.alert} across groups
- Key fairness metrics:
  - **Demographic parity**: Equal positive rates across groups
  - **Equalised odds**: Equal TPR and FPR across groups
  - **Predictive parity**: Equal precision across groups
- [Mathematical impossibility]{.alert}: Can't satisfy all fairness criteria simultaneously (except in special cases)
- Choice of fairness metric is a [value judgment]{.alert}
- Always [disaggregate]{.alert} your metrics by important subgroups
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Fairness in ML](figures/fairness-metrics.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/fairness-metrics.png"}

Source: [Google AI](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/fairness-overview)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Beyond standard metrics
### What else should we measure?

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}

| Dimension | What to measure |
|-----------|-----------------|
| **Robustness** | Performance on adversarial or noisy inputs |
| **Interpretability** | Can humans understand the decisions? |
| **Fairness** | Equitable performance across groups |
| **Privacy** | Does the model leak sensitive information? |
| **Sustainability** | Carbon footprint of training/inference |
| **Social impact** | Effect on communities and society |

<br>

:::{.fragment}
> "What gets measured gets managed—but [not everything that matters can be measured]{.alert}."
:::
:::

# Summary ✅ {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Main takeaways

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 26px;"}

- `r fa('exclamation-triangle')` [Accuracy alone is dangerous]{.alert}—especially for imbalanced classes

- `r fa('balance-scale')` [Precision vs recall]{.alert} trade-off depends on the cost of errors

- `r fa('chart-line')` [Validation is essential]{.alert}—never evaluate on training data

- `r fa('random')` [Cross-validation]{.alert} gives robust estimates with limited data

- `r fa('search')` [Data-centric evaluation]{.alert}: Check for underperforming subgroups and outliers

- `r fa('exchange-alt')` [Distribution shift]{.alert} happens—monitor and adapt your models

- `r fa('users')` [Fairness]{.alert} requires looking beyond aggregate metrics
:::
